doc.title: Hal Galper interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 27, 2022

title: The Fender Rhodes, fusion, and throwing the electric piano in the Hudson
summary: Galper discusses the band's move to the Fender Rhodes and fusion, and explains why he dumped his electric piano in the Hudson River to commit to acoustic piano.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: The LP is a little incorrect. But I think I know what you’re saying because as I listen to Cannonball over the years when it got to that point it sounded to me like they were trying to join in to the fusion thing. And I always wondered was that a conscious decision? Did Cannon and Nat like sit down and have coffee and say this is where we’ve got to go if we want to keep making records, or was that not the case?

I couldn’t say anything. I don’t think I have an opinion about that. Because they were the first ones to use the Fender Rhodes. My piano was directly from Harry Rhodes’ factory. I think the move to the Fender Rhodes was the key to getting into the more fusion kind of thing. Yeah.
You weren’t that fond of it, is that correct?
My first two albums were fusion.

Right. And the Guerilla Band — I guess what made me say that is this little book here. Did you ever see this one? It’s a biodiscography of Cannonball and there’s a quote here from you that I guess appeared in DownBeat after you left the group. “I had pure joy, I wheeled the electric piano down in its case, tossed it in the Hudson River and watched the bubbles come up.”

Yes. I guess I have a tendency to the grand gesture. You know. It was a grand gesture. I, after much thought, realized — and then Cannon kept trying to get me to play the acoustic piano and I wouldn’t do it.
Oh I’m glad you said that.

Because I was very insecure with the acoustic piano. It’s probably a very weak point for me. And I could do what I needed to do on the electric piano but I couldn’t do it on the acoustic. And when I realized that, you know, it wasn’t the acoustic piano that was the problem it was I really had to do the work to get the piano together and I needed to make a commitment, you know, to acoustic piano, and that was my grand gesture. I wheeled it down to the river and threw it in. And since then I haven’t played an electric keyboard. I had to do the work to get out of the piano what I wanted to get out of it. I was just avoiding it.
Was there any advantage with the Rhodes that at least you could compete volume-wise in some situations?
I don’t think it made a difference. Usually on that level of playing the stages are pretty well set up. I never had a problem with that. Yeah.
